prompt: A running process is given a number by the system. What does that number identify?
optionA: The program on disk
optionB: This particular run of the program
optionC: The user who started it
optionD: The position of the program in a menu
correctAnswerText: This particular run of the program
explanation: The number belongs to one run and not to the program. Starting the same program again produces a different number.

prompt: A program is stopped and started again. What happens to the number it was given?
optionA: The same number is reused for the new run
optionB: The number is kept because the program is the same
optionC: The program has no number until it finishes
optionD: The new run receives a different number
correctAnswerText: The new run receives a different number
explanation: Each run is a separate process and gets its own number. Expecting the number to follow the program is what makes stale numbers dangerous later.

prompt: The same program is started three times at once. How many numbers are in play?
optionA: Three, one for each run
optionB: One, since it is the same program
optionC: One, with the three runs sharing it
optionD: None, since only one program is involved
correctAnswerText: Three, one for each run
explanation: Three separate runs mean three separate processes, each with its own number. What they have in common is the program they were started from.

prompt: Why does anything wanting to act on a running process need its number?
optionA: Because the number records how long it has been running
optionB: Because the number states how much memory it may use
optionC: Because the number is how a particular run is named
optionD: Because the number gives its position in the start order
correctAnswerText: Because the number is how a particular run is named
explanation: The number is an address for one run. Without it there would be no way to say which of several runs an instruction applies to.

prompt: A script records the number of a process it started, so that it can stop it later. A colleague says it should record the program name instead. What is the weakness of using the name?
optionA: Program names change too often to rely on
optionB: Several runs of the same program may exist, and the name does not say which is meant
optionC: Program names cannot be recorded in a script
optionD: There is no weakness; the name is more reliable
correctAnswerText: Several runs of the same program may exist, and the name does not say which is meant
explanation: The name identifies the program and the number identifies the run. When only one run exists the two agree, which is why the weakness stays hidden until it does not.

prompt: A process has asked to read from a file and is waiting for the data to arrive. What condition is it in?
optionA: Using the processor
optionB: Ready and waiting for the processor
optionC: Finished
optionD: Blocked, waiting on something outside itself
correctAnswerText: Blocked, waiting on something outside itself
explanation: It cannot proceed until the data arrives, so giving it the processor would achieve nothing. That is what distinguishes this from waiting for a turn.

prompt: A process has everything it needs and is simply waiting for its turn on the processor. What condition is it in?
optionA: Ready, waiting only for the processor
optionB: Blocked, waiting on something outside itself
optionC: Using the processor
optionD: Finished
correctAnswerText: Ready, waiting only for the processor
explanation: Nothing is missing except a turn, so it could run the instant one is available. A blocked process could not.

prompt: Two processes are both described as "not running". What distinguishes them?
optionA: How long each has existed
optionB: How much memory each is using
optionC: Whether each is waiting only for a turn or waiting for something else entirely
optionD: Nothing; not running is a single condition
correctAnswerText: Whether each is waiting only for a turn or waiting for something else entirely
explanation: Adding processors would help one and not the other, which is why the two are kept apart. Lumping them together makes every performance question unanswerable.

prompt: A machine has many processes that are not running, and adding a faster processor makes no difference. What does that suggest about them?
optionA: They were waiting for the processor and the new one is too slow
optionB: They were waiting on something other than the processor
optionC: They have all finished
optionD: The measurement must have been taken incorrectly
correctAnswerText: They were waiting on something other than the processor
explanation: Processes waiting for a turn would have benefited from a faster processor. That nothing changed points at waits the processor cannot end.

prompt: A terminal session is used to start a long-running task. What is the relationship between the two processes?
optionA: The task started the terminal session
optionB: The task runs inside the terminal session as part of it
optionC: The two are unrelated once both are running
optionD: The terminal session started the task
correctAnswerText: The terminal session started the task
explanation: One started the other, and that relationship is recorded. It is a relationship between two separate processes rather than one containing the other.

prompt: When one process starts another, what is recorded about the pair?
optionA: Which one started the other
optionB: Which one will finish first
optionC: That the two must finish together
optionD: That the two share their memory
correctAnswerText: Which one started the other
explanation: The starting relationship is kept and is what lets a process be told how its children fared. Nothing about it forces them to end together.

prompt: A process starts three others. How is it related to them?
optionA: The three are copies of it
optionB: The three run inside it
optionC: It is the starter of all three, and they are unrelated to one another
optionD: The three are related to each other as well as to it
correctAnswerText: It is the starter of all three, and they are unrelated to one another
explanation: Each has the same starter and no relationship to its siblings. Nothing connects them except where they came from.

prompt: A student says that stopping a process automatically stops everything it started, because the children run inside it. What is wrong with the reasoning?
optionA: Nothing; children always stop with their starter
optionB: The children are separate processes; the relationship records who started whom and does not contain them
optionC: The children stop only if they were started recently
optionD: The reasoning is right for programs and wrong for scripts
correctAnswerText: The children are separate processes; the relationship records who started whom and does not contain them
explanation: Containment is the wrong picture. Each child is a process in its own right with its own number and its own life.

prompt: A process that was using the processor asks to read from a slow device. What happens to its condition?
optionA: It moves from using the processor to waiting for a turn
optionB: It keeps the processor until the data arrives
optionC: It finishes
optionD: It moves from using the processor to waiting for the device
correctAnswerText: It moves from using the processor to waiting for the device
explanation: The request cannot be satisfied at once, so holding the processor would waste it. The move is made so that something else can run.

prompt: A process was waiting for data, and the data has now arrived. What condition is it in immediately afterwards?
optionA: Ready, waiting for a turn on the processor
optionB: Using the processor straight away
optionC: Still waiting for the data
optionD: Finished, since its request has been satisfied
correctAnswerText: Ready, waiting for a turn on the processor
explanation: Its obstacle has gone and a free processor has not appeared. It joins the queue for a turn rather than resuming instantly.

prompt: A task is started so that the terminal prompt returns immediately and the task keeps running. How was it started?
optionA: In the foreground, so it holds the terminal
optionB: In the foreground, with the prompt shown early
optionC: In the background, so it does not hold the terminal
optionD: It was not started at all, which is why the prompt returned
correctAnswerText: In the background, so it does not hold the terminal
explanation: Holding the terminal is exactly what a foreground task does. The prompt returning is the observable sign that this one is not.

prompt: A task running in the background prints a message. Where does the message appear?
optionA: Nowhere, since background tasks produce no output
optionB: On the terminal, interleaved with whatever else is there
optionC: In a file, since background output is always redirected
optionD: On the terminal only after the task finishes
correctAnswerText: On the terminal, interleaved with whatever else is there
explanation: Not holding the terminal is not the same as being disconnected from it. The message arrives in the middle of whatever the user is doing, which is why background output is usually sent elsewhere deliberately.

prompt: A process finishes. What does it report about how it went?
optionA: Everything it printed while running
optionB: How long it ran for
optionC: Nothing; a finished process reports nothing
optionD: A value saying whether it succeeded
correctAnswerText: A value saying whether it succeeded
explanation: The reported value is a small signal about success, separate from anything printed. Whatever started it can read that value.

prompt: A task prints several pages of output and then reports failure. What follows?
optionA: It failed, whatever it printed along the way
optionB: It succeeded, since it produced output
optionC: It partly succeeded, in proportion to the output
optionD: The two reports contradict each other and one must be wrong
correctAnswerText: It failed, whatever it printed along the way
explanation: Printing and reporting are different channels and do not contradict each other. A task can do a great deal of work and still not achieve what it was asked to.

prompt: A script runs a task and decides what to do next by reading what the task printed, searching the output for the word "error". The task reports failure through its result value and prints nothing containing that word. The script inspects the printed text and never reads the reported result value. What happens?
optionA: The script detects the failure from the reported value
optionB: The script fails to run, since the task failed
optionC: The script treats the failure as a success, because it never looked at the result
optionD: The script detects the failure from the absence of output
correctAnswerText: The script treats the failure as a success, because it never looked at the result
explanation: The signal was there and the script was reading the wrong channel. Searching output for words is fragile in exactly this way, since the wording is not guaranteed.

prompt: A process is politely asked to stop. What can it do about the request?
optionA: Nothing; it ends immediately
optionB: Notice it and tidy up before ending
optionC: Refuse it permanently and continue as though nothing happened
optionD: Pass the request to whatever started it
correctAnswerText: Notice it and tidy up before ending
explanation: The polite request is deliverable and the process decides how to respond. That opportunity is the whole difference between the two ways of stopping something.

prompt: A process is stopped outright rather than asked. What can it do about it?
optionA: Tidy up first, then end
optionB: Save its work and then end
optionC: Refuse if it is holding a file open
optionD: Nothing; it ends without any opportunity to prepare
correctAnswerText: Nothing; it ends without any opportunity to prepare
explanation: The forced stop is not delivered to the process to be handled. Anything it was part-way through is left as it was.

prompt: A process writing a large file is stopped outright. A colleague expects the file to be either complete or absent. Being stopped outright gives the process no opportunity to finish or to remove what it had already written. What is the likely state of the file?
optionA: Partly written, being neither complete nor absent
optionB: Complete, since the write had started
optionC: Absent, since the process did not finish
optionD: Complete but marked as incomplete
correctAnswerText: Partly written, being neither complete nor absent
explanation: Nothing arranges for a half-written file to be cleaned up unless the process does it, and it was given no chance. Asking politely would have let it either finish or remove the file.

prompt: A process that started another finishes first. What happens to the one it started?
optionA: It stops immediately
optionB: It is suspended until a new starter appears
optionC: It keeps running
optionD: It restarts from the beginning
correctAnswerText: It keeps running
explanation: The relationship records who started whom and does not tie their lives together. The child continues and is adopted by something else.

prompt: A user starts a long task from a terminal and then closes the terminal window. The task is still running afterwards. Is that surprising?
optionA: Yes; closing the terminal should have stopped the task
optionB: No; the task is a separate process and does not end because its starter did
optionC: Yes; the task should have been suspended
optionD: No, but only because the task was started in the background
correctAnswerText: No; the task is a separate process and does not end because its starter did
explanation: Whether it was started in the background affects the terminal rather than survival. Some setups do arrange for tasks to be stopped when a session ends, and that is an arrangement rather than the default behaviour.

prompt: A deployment script starts a server process and then exits. Hours later the server is still running and nobody knows how to stop it, because the script that started it is gone. The server survived its starter and the number it was given was never recorded anywhere. What is the difficulty?
optionA: The server should have stopped when the script exited
optionB: The server cannot be stopped once its starter has gone
optionC: The script must still be running somewhere
optionD: The server is running with no record of its number, so it has to be found before it can be stopped
correctAnswerText: The server is running with no record of its number, so it has to be found before it can be stopped
explanation: Survival is the expected behaviour and the missing record is the problem. A listing of running processes will find it; recording the number at start time would have avoided the search.

prompt: A process ends. What happens to the number it was using?
optionA: It becomes available for a later process
optionB: It is retired and never used again
optionC: It is kept in case the process restarts
optionD: It is transferred to whatever started the process
correctAnswerText: It becomes available for a later process
explanation: Numbers are a finite supply and are reissued once free. That is why one recorded some time ago may now name something entirely different.

prompt: A number was written into a file yesterday when a process was started. What can be concluded from it today?
optionA: That the same process still has it
optionB: That no process has it now
optionC: That some process had that number yesterday; nothing certain about today
optionD: That the process finished, since the number was recorded
correctAnswerText: That some process had that number yesterday; nothing certain about today
explanation: The number may name the original process, a completely different one, or nothing at all. Checking what is actually running is what distinguishes the three.

prompt: A monitoring script records a number at start time and checks each hour whether a process with that number is running, reporting the service as healthy if one is. A number becomes available when its process ends and may then be given to something unrelated. What is wrong with the check?
optionA: The check is sound, since the number is unique
optionB: A different process may now hold that number, so the check can report health when the service has died
optionC: The check will report failure even when the service is running
optionD: The check should be run more often than hourly
correctAnswerText: A different process may now hold that number, so the check can report health when the service has died
explanation: Presence of the number is not presence of the service. Comparing the program name as well, or asking the service itself, is what makes the check mean something.

prompt: A listing of running processes is produced. What does it describe?
optionA: The situation continuously as it changes
optionB: Every process that has run since the machine started
optionC: Every process that will run today
optionD: The situation at the moment it was taken
correctAnswerText: The situation at the moment it was taken
explanation: The listing is a snapshot. Anything that started or ended after it was taken is not reflected in it.

prompt: A process a user expected to find does not appear in a listing. What follows?
optionA: It was not running at that moment; whether it ran earlier is a separate question
optionB: It has never run
optionC: It is running but hidden
optionD: It has finished successfully
correctAnswerText: It was not running at that moment; whether it ran earlier is a separate question
explanation: Absence from a snapshot says only that it was not there then. It may have ended a second earlier, successfully or otherwise.

prompt: A listing shows one process using a very high share of the processor. A team concludes it has been overloading the machine all morning. The listing describes the instant it was taken and says nothing about the hours before it. What does the listing support?
optionA: That the process has been busy all morning
optionB: That the process is faulty
optionC: That the process was busy at that instant, and nothing about the morning
optionD: That the machine is short of processors
correctAnswerText: That the process was busy at that instant, and nothing about the morning
explanation: One instant is one instant. Sampling repeatedly, or consulting a record kept over time, is what would support a claim about the morning.

prompt: A process is politely asked to stop and does not. It is waiting for a reply from a machine that is not responding. Why has the request had no effect?
optionA: The request was not delivered
optionB: It cannot act on the request while it is blocked waiting
optionC: The process has crashed and can no longer receive anything
optionD: The process is refusing the request deliberately
correctAnswerText: It cannot act on the request while it is blocked waiting
explanation: A blocked process is not running any instructions, so it cannot notice the request. When the wait ends it would act on it, and the wait may not end.

prompt: A process ignores a polite stop request. It is mid-way through writing a file. Forcing it would end it at once and would leave the file part-written, while waiting risks waiting indefinitely. What is the trade being made?
optionA: Nothing; forcing it is always correct here
optionB: Nothing; waiting is always correct here
optionC: Whether the process is important enough to keep
optionD: Ending it now at the cost of a part-written file, against waiting for a wait that may not end
correctAnswerText: Ending it now at the cost of a part-written file, against waiting for a wait that may not end
explanation: Both options have a real cost and the stem states both. Which is right depends on whether the part-written file can be recovered from, which is a question about this file.

prompt: An administrator stops a process using a number from a note made last week. The command reports success, and an unrelated service goes down. What most likely happened?
optionA: The number now belonged to the unrelated service
optionB: The command was mistyped
optionC: The original process had a dependency on the service
optionD: The command failed silently and something else caused the outage
correctAnswerText: The number now belonged to the unrelated service
explanation: The command reporting success means it found and stopped a process with that number. The number was reissued between last week and today.

prompt: A cleanup job stops every process whose number appears in a list built at midnight. It runs at six, reports every stop as successful, and two unrelated services are found stopped. The job reported success for every number, and success means a process with that number was found and stopped. What happened?
optionA: The job failed and the outage has another cause
optionB: The original processes had been restarted with the same numbers
optionC: Some of those numbers had been reissued to other processes in the six hours since the list was built
optionD: The list was built incorrectly at midnight
correctAnswerText: Some of those numbers had been reissued to other processes in the six hours since the list was built
explanation: Every stop succeeding is the evidence: each number named a live process. The list was correct when it was built and had six hours to go stale.

prompt: A process created a temporary file at the start of its run and removes it just before finishing. It is stopped outright halfway through. What is left behind?
optionA: Nothing; temporary files are always cleaned up
optionB: The temporary file, since the removal never happened
optionC: The temporary file, but it will be removed automatically later
optionD: Nothing, since the process did not finish
correctAnswerText: The temporary file, since the removal never happened
explanation: Cleaning up was something the process was going to do and it was not given the chance. Nothing else knows the file was temporary.

prompt: A process holds a lock while it works and releases it when it finishes. It is stopped outright. Releasing the lock was something the process did on finishing, and it was given no opportunity to do anything. What is the state of the lock?
optionA: Released, since the process is gone
optionB: Released after a short delay
optionC: Held by whatever started the process
optionD: Still held, with no process holding it, so anything waiting for it waits indefinitely
correctAnswerText: Still held, with no process holding it, so anything waiting for it waits indefinitely
explanation: A lock that outlives its holder is the classic consequence of forcing a stop. Locks that are released automatically when the holder disappears exist and have to be built that way deliberately.

prompt: A service is restarted every night by stopping it outright and starting it again. It has worked for months. It writes to a file continuously, and the stop can land at any point in a write. What is the position?
optionA: It has been fortunate; a stop landing mid-write will eventually corrupt the file
optionB: It is safe, since months of success is strong evidence
optionC: It is safe, since restarts are a normal operation
optionD: It is unsafe, and the corruption has certainly already happened
correctAnswerText: It has been fortunate; a stop landing mid-write will eventually corrupt the file
explanation: Months without incident is evidence that the window is narrow rather than that it is absent. Asking politely first, and forcing only if the request is ignored, closes it.

prompt: A process starts a child and finishes immediately. The child runs for an hour and then fails. The starter has already finished, so there is nothing left to receive a report of how the child fared. What happens to the information that it failed?
optionA: It is reported to whatever adopted the child
optionB: It is reported to the user who started the original process
optionC: It has nowhere to go, so the failure is unreported unless the child recorded it itself
optionD: It is kept until the starter is restarted
correctAnswerText: It has nowhere to go, so the failure is unreported unless the child recorded it itself
explanation: The reported value goes to whatever is waiting for it and nothing is. This is why long-running work started this way has to write its own record of what happened.

prompt: A process finishes successfully in one second, every time it is run, and a monitoring system that checks once a minute never sees it running. The process exists for one second in every sixty and the check samples one instant per minute. What does the monitoring establish?
optionA: That the process is never running
optionB: Almost nothing; a process this short is unlikely to be caught by a check this infrequent
optionC: That the process fails to start
optionD: That the process finishes too quickly to be useful
correctAnswerText: Almost nothing; a process this short is unlikely to be caught by a check this infrequent
explanation: The absence is what sampling predicts rather than evidence of anything. Recording each run as it happens is what would answer the question the monitoring was trying to answer.

prompt: A process is consuming a great deal of processor time and is part-way through writing a report file. It is not blocked and it responds to requests. It is responsive and mid-write, so it can be asked and can tidy up. How should it be stopped?
optionA: Force it, since it is consuming resources now
optionB: Force it, since polite requests are unreliable
optionC: Leave it, since stopping it risks the file
optionD: Ask it politely, so that it can finish or remove the part-written file
correctAnswerText: Ask it politely, so that it can finish or remove the part-written file
explanation: Both conditions for the polite route are present. Forcing would end it faster and leave the file in the state this family exists to warn about.

prompt: A process is blocked waiting on a machine that will not respond, holding no files open, and is preventing a deployment. It has been asked politely and has not reacted. It holds no files open and cannot act on a polite request while it is blocked. What should be done?
optionA: Force it, since nothing is at risk and the polite route cannot work while it is blocked
optionB: Keep waiting, since the polite request may still be acted on
optionC: Restart the machine, since the process cannot be stopped
optionD: Ask politely again, in case the first request was lost
correctAnswerText: Force it, since nothing is at risk and the polite route cannot work while it is blocked
explanation: The two facts together settle it: the polite route is unavailable and forcing costs nothing here. Repeating a request that cannot be noticed changes nothing.

prompt: A team wants a script to stop a service reliably. A colleague proposes forcing it immediately, because polite requests sometimes go unanswered. The service tidies up when asked politely, and forcing gives it no opportunity to do so. What is the better arrangement?
optionA: Force immediately, since it is reliable
optionB: Ask politely and never force, since forcing risks the tidy-up
optionC: Ask politely, wait a stated period, and force only if it has not ended
optionD: Ask politely twice before forcing
correctAnswerText: Ask politely, wait a stated period, and force only if it has not ended
explanation: Forcing immediately gives up the tidy-up in every case to handle the case where it is needed. Never forcing leaves the script unable to finish when a process is stuck.

prompt: A process must be stopped, and a colleague proposes stopping everything started by the same session to be thorough. That session also started an unrelated long-running job that has been running for hours. Stopping everything from the session would also stop the unrelated job, which nobody asked to stop. What follows?
optionA: Stop everything from the session, since thoroughness is safer
optionB: Only the intended process should be stopped, since the broader action reaches something unrelated
optionC: Stop everything from the session, since the jobs are related by their starter
optionD: Stop nothing, since the two cannot be separated
correctAnswerText: Only the intended process should be stopped, since the broader action reaches something unrelated
explanation: Sharing a starter is not sharing a purpose. The two jobs are separate processes and can be addressed separately by their own numbers.

prompt: A team can stop a stuck process now, losing the state that would explain why it stuck, or leave it and investigate while it is still stuck. The service is degraded but working, and the stuck state is the only evidence of why this keeps happening. What should decide?
optionA: Stopping it, since service always comes first
optionB: Investigating, since understanding always comes first
optionC: Neither; the process should be left indefinitely
optionD: Whether the recurring cause is worth more than restoring full service immediately
correctAnswerText: Whether the recurring cause is worth more than restoring full service immediately
explanation: Both have a real cost and the stem supplies what makes it a genuine choice: the service is degraded rather than down, and this is the only chance to see the cause. Capturing the state and then stopping it is often the way to have both.

prompt: A container platform gives each running container an identifier, records which one launched which, and reports a result value when one ends. A container is launched by another that then exits. The platform records the launching relationship and nothing in the description says a launched container ends with its launcher. What happens to the launched container?
optionA: It keeps running, since nothing described ties its life to its launcher
optionB: It stops, since its launcher has gone
optionC: It is suspended until the launcher returns
optionD: It cannot be determined without knowing the platform
correctAnswerText: It keeps running, since nothing described ties its life to its launcher
explanation: The described model is the process model under another name, and the same conclusion follows from it. A platform could arrange otherwise and this description does not.

prompt: A job scheduler gives each run an identifier and reuses identifiers once a run has completed. A dashboard stores identifiers and displays the status of whatever currently holds each one. Identifiers are reused after completion and the dashboard looks up whatever holds one now. What will the dashboard eventually show?
optionA: Nothing, once the original run has completed
optionB: The status of the original run, retained after completion
optionC: The status of an unrelated later run, presented as though it were the original
optionD: An error, since the identifier no longer exists
correctAnswerText: The status of an unrelated later run, presented as though it were the original
explanation: This is identifier reuse in a different setting and produces the same fault. Recording the start time alongside the identifier is what lets the dashboard tell the two apart.

prompt: A platform sends a shutdown request to a running task and stops it outright if it has not ended within thirty seconds. A team writes a task that takes two minutes to save its state on shutdown. The task needs two minutes to tidy up and will be stopped outright after thirty seconds. What will happen?
optionA: It will be allowed to finish saving, since it responded to the request
optionB: It will be stopped part-way through saving, every time
optionC: It will be stopped only if the platform is under load
optionD: It will never receive the shutdown request
correctAnswerText: It will be stopped part-way through saving, every time
explanation: Responding to the request is not the same as finishing within the window. Saving faster, or saving continuously so that shutdown has little to do, is what fits the platform.

prompt: A team must decide whether a background worker should record its own outcome to a log or rely on the system that started it to capture the result value. The starter exits immediately after launching the worker, so nothing is waiting to receive a result value. Which should they choose?
optionA: Rely on the starter, since result values are the standard mechanism
optionB: Rely on the starter, since logs can be lost
optionC: Neither is needed, since failures are always visible
optionD: The worker should record its own outcome, since nothing will be there to receive a reported result
correctAnswerText: The worker should record its own outcome, since nothing will be there to receive a reported result
explanation: The reported value goes to whatever is waiting, and the stem states that nothing will be. Where the starter waits, relying on the result value would be the simpler choice.
